title: How I use AI for investment research without getting fooled by it
author: Entire-Print4239
selftext:
I use AI for investment research. The goal is alpha — insight the market hasn't priced yet. This post is about the system I built to get there, but let me start with what it's not: it will not tell you "click here and the AI picks tomorrow's winner".I know a lot of people want that holy grail. I don't have it, and I don't believe it exists.

The first thing you learn doing this is almost embarrassingly simple: if you just ask an AI about a stock, all you get back is analyst consensus — public, mass-produced, edge-free. Consensus is the exact opposite of alpha, and you don't need AI for it; it's on every finance app. The only use of AI that's worth anything is forcing it to work like a human analyst: gather the primary sources, reason through them step by step, reach its own conclusion — no step skipped, every step chained to evidence so it can't get lazy. Fresh reasoning with its brain, not a summary of everyone else's.

But the moment you actually do that, you hit three problems, each worse than you'd expect:

1. It agrees with you. Leak the slightest hint of what you want to believe, and it starts building the case for you — fast and well. This is a hundred times more dangerous than it arguing back.
2. It makes up numbers. When data is missing, it doesn't say "I don't know." It says something plausible.
3. The biggest problem is me. Once a human gets a conclusion that supports what they already think, they stop checking. AI drops the cost of that human weakness to zero.

So the core of the system isn't making the AI smarter. It's building accountability — for the AI and for myself. Four mechanisms:

1. Blind calls. Before I say anything about where I'm leaning, the AI has to write down its own verdict and lock it in. Then I state mine. Both go on file, side by side. This stops the AI from following me, stops me from anchoring on the AI, and builds a two-sided track record — over time you learn who's actually more reliable, and on which kinds of questions each of us fails.

2. A prediction ledger. Every judgment has to be broken into dated, checkable predictions: "metric X above threshold Y by date Z, with probability P." A script flags them when they come due, and both of us get scored. Opinions are cheap to hold; predictions expire. There are 50 open on the books right now. Nobody gets to quietly forget being wrong.

3. Kill screens — check the cheap deaths first. 80% of stocks can be killed cheaply, and tokens and hours are costs too. My first five deep-dives: four ended in rejection, and every kill shot was one or two facts I could have checked in an afternoon. All that deep work, wasted. New rule: before any full workup, spend half a day on the historically most common causes of death — what the current price already implies, whether the thesis's key claim actually exists in the primary filings, accounting red flags. Only survivors earn the full treatment.

4. Adversarial review. Before real money moves, several AI analysts — each running a different investment philosophy — get a neutral evidence pack, can't see each other, and independently redo the entire research from scratch. Their job is to find holes in mine. They don't know my conclusion, so they don't pull punches.

Does it work? Here's one save: I had an AI assemble a segment-level profit model, and somewhere in the multi-step arithmetic it slipped in a 10x unit error. Every individual step read smoothly — you could not spot it by reading. But the system has a gate: segment estimates must sum back into the company's verified reported totals, or nothing enters the table. The check ran, the sum was off by an order of magnitude, blocked on the spot. New rule since that day: arithmetic belongs to scripts, always. The AI is only allowed to argue about assumptions.

Honestly, in the moment it got caught, I felt almost nothing — relief, then back to work. Later I realized that almost nothing is the whole point: a good system makes near-disasters boring. You don't want to catch errors by being sharp-eyed every time. You want errors to walk into the gate on their own.

Last thing: none of this is really about stocks. Any decision where being wrong costs you something — picking a job offer, a product bet, a major purchase — is the same problem. AI doesn't lack capability. It lacks accountability, and you have to build that yourself.

This system has only ever had one client: me. I'm looking for one or two people with a real decision on their hands — I'll build you a version for free, in exchange for your feedback.
